claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed iron oxide film.
The naturally formed iron oxide film on as-received Q235 steel is heterogeneous.
The uniformity and adhesion of the native iron oxide film determine whether Q235 steel retains corrosion protection or degrades during aggressive salt exposure.
Chemical cleaning followed by controlled thermal annealing in a protective atmosphere can regenerate a more uniform and adherent oxide film.
High temperatures enhance diffusion and oxidation processes.
A uniformly grown and adherent oxide film minimizes defects and forms a continuous barrier against corrosive salts at 700–900 °C.
A nonuniform or defective oxide film provides sites for localized corrosion breakdown.
Localized breakdown of a defective oxide film causes increased mass change and degradation.
Q235 samples with a more uniform and adherent engineered oxide film will show lower mass change than untreated samples during aggressive salt exposure.
Q235 samples with a more uniform and adherent engineered oxide film will show fewer localized corrosion sites and better corrosion resistance than untreated samples.
The corrosion-performance difference between treated and untreated samples will be less pronounced at room temperature than at 700–900 °C.
Slower oxidation kinetics at room temperature cause the predicted treatment effect to be less pronounced there.
The proposed mechanism is specific to Q235 steel and may not apply to significantly alloyed steels or HEAs because they can possess additional passivation mechanisms.

Failure of the engineered-film group to show a statistically significant reduction in mass change and localized corrosion relative to untreated controls at high temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
